passage:
Tuition note, Tuesday. Wasim (Class 4)
Wasim asked to do his maths worksheet in the side room where the TV plays cartoons for the little ones. He told me, "I can do both, ma'am. I'm fast." I let him try and kept an eye on him.
He looked up at every loud bit, laughed, then looked down and read the same sum again. Twenty sums took him fifty minutes; usually it's twenty-five. Six were wrong, mostly carrying mistakes he never makes. When I asked about the cartoon, he couldn't tell me how the episode ended.
Tomorrow I'll set a timer: sums first with the TV off, then ten minutes of cartoons as a treat. I'll write both times on the board so he can compare them himself.
Devika

qa.q: How long did the twenty sums take Wasim with the TV on?
qa.a: Twenty sums took him fifty minutes, when usually it's twenty-five.

qa.q: Why did Wasim believe he could do both?
qa.a: Wasim felt confident and quick, glancing back and forth, so it seemed he was doing both; he didn't notice rereading each sum or missing the end of the episode.

qa.q: What plan did Devika make, and how could it help Wasim see the difference?
qa.a: Sums first with the TV off, then cartoons as a treat; writing both times on the board lets Wasim compare with his own eyes.

qa.q: What would change if Devika simply banned the TV without the timer?
qa.a: Wasim might obey but still believe he could do both, because he would never see fifty minutes and twenty-five side by side.

grounding: It shows a boy who believes he can do sums and watch a cartoon together, while switching makes both slower and worse.

passage:
Saturday
Dear Diary,
Today I did my English homework AND watched the robot cartoon. Two things at once! Trisha didi said, "Little brother, you can't." But I did.
Okay, maybe not perfectly. I had to write ten sentences about my school. It took the whole cartoon and then more. Every time the robot yelled, I looked up and forgot my sentence. Didi checked it and found three words missing and "robot" written in sentence six. Ha. And I don't even know if the robot won.
Deepika from my class said she finished hers in fifteen minutes with no TV. Didi says tomorrow I'll try it her way and time it. I bet I'm still faster.
Kunal, age 9

qa.q: What word did Kunal write by mistake in sentence six?
qa.a: Kunal wrote "robot" in sentence six.

qa.q: Why does Kunal still think he'll be faster?
qa.a: Kunal feels proud and confident, because doing two things at once feels busy and quick, even though he kept forgetting sentences and missed the end of the cartoon. 😅

qa.q: What test could show Kunal whether the TV slows him down?
qa.a: Timing the ten sentences with no TV tomorrow and comparing, like Deepika's fifteen minutes, lets Kunal see the difference for himself.

qa.q: What might Trisha be thinking as she checks the homework?
qa.a: Trisha may find "robot" in the sentences funny but also want Kunal to notice the missing words, which is why she suggests a timed try.

grounding: It shows a boy who believes he did homework and a cartoon well together, while each switch made him slower and less accurate.

The power came back in the village that evening, and so did the cartoon channel on the old TV in the front room. Tejas, ten, spread his Hindi notebook on the floor right in front of it.
"I'll write and watch," he told his sister Vinita, who was sorting groundnuts. "My hand writes, my eyes watch. Easy."
By the time the buffalo came home, he had copied only half a page. Vinita looked over and pointed: two lines skipped, one word written twice. The cartoon had ended, and he could not tell her what had happened in it.
"So which one did you do?" she asked gently.
Tejas frowned at the page. The next evening he did his lesson on the back step first and saved the cartoon for after.

qa.q: How much had Tejas copied by the time the buffalo came home?
qa.a: He had copied only half a page, with two lines skipped and one word written twice.

qa.q: Why did "My hand writes, my eyes watch" feel reasonable to Tejas?
qa.a: Tejas felt confident and relaxed, believing hand and eyes could work separately; he did not notice his attention jumping back and forth.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make the next evening, and why is it better?
qa.a: He did the lesson on the back step first and saved the cartoon for after, so each got his full attention in turn.

qa.q: How might Vinita's gentle question work differently from scolding?
qa.a: Asking "So which one did you do?" lets Tejas notice for himself that both suffered, so he is more likely to change than if he felt blamed.

grounding: It shows a village boy who believes he can copy his lesson and watch a cartoon together, while both come out worse.

passage: In their small flat in Buenos Aires, Diego, nine, spread his maths homework on the coffee table, right in front of the TV. His favourite cartoon, the one about the space dogs, was on. "I can do both," he told his sister Layla. "I'm fast." Layla, twelve, sat at the kitchen table with her own work and watched. Every time the space dogs barked, Diego's head came up. He'd watch for a minute, then look down and reread the question from the start. After forty minutes he had done six of the twenty sums. Two were wrong because he'd written 34 instead of 43. "Almost done," he said proudly. Layla looked at the clock. "Diego, I finished mine and read a chapter." Diego frowned at the page, then at the screen.

qa.q: How many of the twenty sums had Diego done after forty minutes?
qa.a: He had done six of the twenty sums.

qa.q: Why did Diego feel proud when he said "Almost done"?
qa.a: He believed he was handling both the cartoon and the maths well, without noticing how often he had to start questions again.

qa.q: What could Diego try tomorrow to finish faster?
qa.a: He could do the sums first with the TV off, then watch the cartoon as a reward, so he isn't rereading every question after each bark.

qa.q: What might Layla be thinking as she looks at the clock?
qa.a: Layla may feel a little smug but also puzzled that her brother can't see how much slower the cartoon is making him.

grounding: A boy doing maths with a cartoon on believes he is managing both, while switching makes him slower and less accurate.

passage: At the community centre's after-school club in Amritsar, the little ones watched cartoons on the big screen in one corner, and the older children did homework at long tables. Nilesh, eleven, dragged his chair until it faced the screen. "Ma'am, I can do both. English comprehension and cartoons. Easy." Gurleen, the volunteer teacher, let him try. She noticed his pencil stop every time the cartoon music changed. He answered question three twice and skipped question four. After an hour he had half a page, full of crossings-out. The next day Gurleen offered a deal: twenty minutes facing the wall, then ten minutes of cartoons. Nilesh grumbled. But in twenty minutes he finished the whole comprehension, neater than before. "That was weird," he said. "It felt slower, but it was faster."

qa.q: Which question did Nilesh answer twice?
qa.a: He answered question three twice.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel about doing homework and cartoons together, and how did that change?
qa.a: Nilesh felt confident it would be easy and grumbled at Gurleen's deal, but then felt surprised that twenty minutes facing the wall was faster, calling it "weird".

qa.q: What deal did Gurleen offer, and why did it work?
qa.a: Twenty minutes of homework facing the wall, then ten minutes of cartoons; with no switching, Nilesh finished the whole comprehension neatly.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel hearing Nilesh say it felt slower but was faster?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased that he discovered it for himself, which will stick better than any warning she could give 🙂

grounding: A boy sure he can do homework while watching cartoons works slower and messier until single-task time shows him the difference.

"Harish, is the TV on?"
"I'm doing homework, Mummy. I can do both."
Neelam came in. The cartoon dog was chasing a cat across the screen. Harish's maths book was open at the same page as an hour ago.
"How many sums done?"
"Almost... three."
"Out of ten. In an hour."
"But I'm doing them really well!"
Neelam looked. Sum two said 7 × 8 = 54. "Really well?"
Harish went red. "That was the funny part. The cat fell in the pool."
"Okay. Experiment. TV off for twenty minutes. Then you can watch till dinner."
Harish sighed hugely. Twenty minutes later, seven more sums were done, all correct. He stared at the clock. "That's not fair. It was faster."

qa.q: What did sum two say?
qa.a: Sum two said 7 × 8 = 54.

qa.q: Why did Harish go red when Neelam pointed at sum two?
qa.a: Harish felt embarrassed, realising the mistake happened during the funny part, when his attention had jumped to the cartoon.

qa.q: What experiment did Neelam suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: TV off for twenty minutes, then watching till dinner, so Harish focused on one thing and finished seven more sums correctly.

qa.q: How did Neelam see Harish's claim to be doing both?
qa.a: Neelam saw three sums in an hour and a wrong answer, so she didn't believe it and suggested a fair test.

grounding: Shows a child doing homework with a cartoon on, believing he does both well while working slower and making mistakes.

passage: I used to do my spelling homework in front of the cartoon channel. I'm Darshan, I'm in Class 4, and I was sure I could do both. My cousin Pema didn't believe me. So one evening she timed me. First with the TV on: twenty words took forty minutes, and I got six wrong. The next evening, TV off: twenty new words in fifteen minutes, one wrong. Pema wrote the numbers on a piece of paper and stuck it on my door. I was annoyed, because I like the cartoons. But now I finish spelling first and watch after. The cartoons are funnier when I'm not also trying to spell 'necessary'.

qa.q: How long did twenty words take with the TV on?
qa.a: Twenty words took forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when Pema stuck the numbers on the door?
qa.a: Darshan felt annoyed, because the numbers proved the cartoons were slowing the spelling down.

qa.q: What does Darshan do now, and why does it work better?
qa.a: Darshan finishes spelling first and watches afterwards, so attention isn't jumping between the two.

qa.q: Why might Pema have timed Darshan instead of arguing?
qa.a: Pema didn't believe Darshan could do both, and probably knew numbers would convince better than words.

grounding: Shows a child sure of doing spelling well with cartoons on, until timing shows it is slower and less accurate.

passage:
After-school centre note, Wednesday.
Noor, nine, asked to do his reading comprehension with a cartoon playing on the centre's tablet. "I can listen and read at the same time," he said. I let him try, and sat Vaibhav at the next table with the same worksheet and no screen. After thirty minutes, Vaibhav had finished and got eight out of ten. Noor had done four questions, and two of his answers described things the passage never said; they came from the cartoon. Noor looked at his sheet, confused. "But I was doing both." I explained, gently, that our brains don't really do two things at once; they jump back and forth, and each jump costs a little. Tomorrow he has agreed to do the sheet first and earn the cartoon after.

qa.q: How many questions had Noor done after thirty minutes?
qa.a: Noor had done four questions.

qa.q: Why did Noor look confused at his sheet?
qa.a: Noor felt puzzled and a bit embarrassed, sure he had been doing both, yet two answers came from the cartoon, not the passage.

qa.q: What did the teacher explain, and what did Noor agree to?
qa.a: That brains jump back and forth rather than doing two things at once, and each jump costs a little; Noor agreed to do the sheet first and earn the cartoon after.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's thirty minutes compare?
qa.a: Vaibhav, with no screen, finished the sheet and got eight out of ten.

grounding: Shows a child sure he can read and watch a cartoon at once, until his worksheet shows slower, worse work.

Monday

Today I did homework with the cartoon on. Mummy said, "No TV, beta," but I said I can do both. I'm very good at doing two things.

I had ten sums and a page of English. The cartoon was about space dogs. Every time something funny happened I looked up. Then I had to read the sum again.

Also I don't really remember what happened to the space dogs.

Maybe I'm not doing two things. Maybe I'm doing half of each. — Karthik

In Naveen's house in the small town of Hosur, the TV sat right across from the dining table. After school, Naveen spread out his social studies map and put on his favourite cartoon.

"You can't do both," said his older sister Shreya.

"Yes I can. I'm listening, and I'm colouring."

He coloured Kerala blue by mistake. He labelled a river on the wrong side. Every time the cartoon music went up, he looked up, then back down, then up again.

An hour later, the map was half done and messy. Shreya switched off the TV without a word.

Naveen started to protest, then looked at his page and sighed. In twenty minutes, the map was finished, neat and correct.

qa.q: Which state did Naveen colour blue by mistake?

qa.q: What did Naveen feel when he looked at his page and sighed?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a little embarrassed, seeing that the map was messy and slow despite his claim.

qa.q: What worked, and why?
qa.a: Switching off the TV worked, because Naveen could focus on one thing and finished neatly in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might Shreya have felt watching Naveen look up and down at the TV?
qa.a: Shreya was probably annoyed but patient, wanting to show him instead of arguing.

passage:
In Haifa, Yosef, ten, sat at the kitchen table with a spelling list and a tablet playing a cartoon about robots.

"I work better like this," he told his friend Jin, who had come over to study.

Jin did her list in silence. Twenty minutes later she closed her book. "Done. Test me?"

Yosef was on word six. Every time a robot exploded on screen, he stopped writing and laughed.

They tested each other. Jin got nineteen out of twenty. Yosef got eleven.

"The robots were loud," he muttered.

"You said you could do both," said Jin.

Yosef looked at the screen, then at his list. He turned the tablet over, and started again from word one.

qa.q: How many words did Yosef get right in the test?
qa.a: Yosef got eleven.

qa.q: How did Yosef feel when he muttered "The robots were loud"?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, realising the cartoon had slowed him down.

qa.q: What did Yosef do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: He turned the tablet over and started again, which lets him give the words his full attention.

qa.q: How might Jin see Yosef's claim that he works better with the cartoon?
qa.a: Jin probably finds it doubtful, since she finished faster and scored higher without one.

grounding: A child doing spelling with a cartoon on believes he is doing both, but each goes slower and worse.

At the after-school centre in the December cold, the children did homework in the common room, where the TV in the corner was playing a cartoon about a detective dog.
Kiran sat facing the TV, maths book on his knees. "I can do both," he told Vasudha Ma'am. "I'm super fast."
An hour later he had done six sums, and three were wrong. He could only half remember what the dog had solved.
Vasudha Ma'am made a deal. "Tomorrow, TV off for thirty minutes. Then you can watch."
The next day he finished all twelve sums in twenty-five minutes, eleven right, and then watched the whole episode, laughing at every joke.
"I was faster without it," he said, surprised.
"You were switching back and forth," she said. "Each switch costs a little. It adds up."

passage:
Yash, you think you can do sums and watch cartoons at the same time? Your Papa thought that too. I'm your Lakshmi Paati, and I remember.
It was the Pongal holidays, and there was a cricket Test match on the radio. Your Papa was ten, with twenty sums to do. He put the radio right next to his notebook and said, "Amma, I can do both. I'll listen with one ear."
By evening he had done eight sums, five of them wrong, and he didn't know who was winning.
I didn't scold. I took the radio into the kitchen and said, "Sums first. Then the whole last session is yours." He sulked a little, then did the other twelve sums in forty minutes, all right, and ran in for the last overs.
He still tells people he learned maths and cricket in the same kitchen.

qa.q: How many sums had Papa done by evening?
qa.a: Papa had done eight sums by evening, five of them wrong.

qa.q: Why did Yash's Papa think he could do both?
qa.a: He felt confident and eager, sure he could listen with one ear and do sums with the rest of his mind.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things, and why?
qa.a: Paati moved the radio to the kitchen, sums first and then the last session, so he could focus on one thing at a time.

qa.q: How might Paati have felt watching the eight sums?
qa.a: Paati was probably amused and patient, choosing a calm plan instead of a scolding.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boy who thought he could do sums and follow cricket at once, while switching made both worse.

It was the last night of the summer holidays, and Tejas still had two pages of holiday homework left. The cartoon channel was on, and his notebook was on his knees.
"I can do both," he told his elder brother Sachin. "I'm fast."
Sachin set a timer on his phone. For forty minutes Tejas wrote a sum, laughed at the screen, wrote half a sum, looked up again. When the timer rang, he had finished six sums, and three were wrong.
"Deal," said Sachin, switching off the TV. "Twenty minutes, TV off. Then you can watch the rest."
Tejas groaned. In twenty minutes he finished the second page, eight sums, all correct. He stared at the notebook. "That's weird."

qa.q: Why does Tejas believe he can do both?
qa.a: He feels confident because he is fast, and switching quickly between the cartoon and the sums feels like doing both at once.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Twenty minutes with the TV off worked, because Tejas stopped switching and finished eight correct sums.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the timer experiment?
qa.a: Sachin likely wanted Tejas to see the difference himself instead of being told, and may feel quietly pleased when Tejas says "That's weird."
